confounds: Diagnosed users have approximately 19% more retained posts and words, creating a major activity and collection confound.
The four-block persistence checks use source order, not calibrated dates; temporal drift and topic changes may remain.
Portuguese slang, spelling variation, contractions, accents, emojis, and polysemous negation/pronoun forms reduce rule precision.
Punctuation, laughter, capitalization, and message length may primarily reflect demographic, subcommunity, fandom, device, or account-type differences.
Labels are outcomes to explain; none of these associations establishes causality or clinical diagnostic validity.
The diagnosed class is much smaller than the control class (618 vs 5464 users), so small effects require conservative weighting and validation.

negative_results: Overall lexical diversity was essentially null: mean per-post TTR was 96.66% diagnosed vs 96.96% control; fixed-50-post pooled TTR was 58.05% vs 58.33%.
Tense proxies were weak: past-marker posts were 12.67% vs 12.60%; future-marker posts were 10.88% vs 10.23%, with almost no token-rate difference.
Second-person markers were not stable: 9.11% diagnosed vs 9.43% control posts, with only 2/4 folds favoring diagnosed.
No useful link/hashtag signal: no hashtags and only three external-link strings in approximately 3.27 million posts.

The clean pooled rate of the exact pronoun “eu” was higher for diagnosed users (2.87 vs 2.07 per 100 tokens), but this is token-weighted and was not promoted without validated macro-user and fold-level support.
Coarse quotation, lyrics, news, and advocacy cues were too sparse or ambiguous for a reliable class difference.
